By surface analysis, knekke (“to crack, break”) + brød (“bread”).

1004564.etyen:
From the name of the farm Grevæg in Trøgstad, now in Indre Østfold.
The name is first recorded circa 1400 as Grafegg, and later as Graffeg in 1593, Greffegh in 1604 and 1612, and Greweg in 1723. The second element is Old Norse egg (“edge, ridge”). The first element is uncertain. The oldest form may contain Old Norse grǫf (“pit, hollow”), although it has alternatively been connected with Old Norse gref (“spade”), possibly referring to the shape of the ridge.

en.g: a flexible or articulated-frame harrow; a shallow-working harrow made of two to four connected rows of short wooden blocks, each carrying one or two wooden or iron tines, designed to follow uneven or stony ground and used to level fields and cover seed or manure

1004820.etyen:
From ledd (“joint, link; articulated section”) + harv (“harrow”), literally “link harrow”.
Parallel formations include Danish ledharve, Swedish ledharv and länkharv, and German Gliederegge (“flexible harrow, articulated-frame harrow”).

en.g: unacceptable, bad, yucky; regarded jokingly as objectionable or undesirable
x: olje er fysjom og gass er æsj
Oil is yucky and gas is icky.

1005076.etyen: From fysj (“yuck, ugh”), with an expressive ending of uncertain origin. Det Norske Akademis ordbok suggests that the form may have been modelled on bråttom (“in a hurry”). Store norske leksikon additionally suggests that it may have arisen humorously during the Samnorsk debates of the 1950s, with -om imitating older Norwegian Nynorsk dative forms; alternatively, it may likewise have been influenced by Swedish bråttom (“in a hurry”).
